Issued at 159 PM EST Wed Nov 11 2026

Early afternoon RAP analysis shows surface low pressure around 
1010mb skirting south of the Great Lakes while 1028 mb is over 
northern Manitoba. Aloft, the 500 mb pattern consists of a strong 
ridge over the US Rockies to Canadian High Plains and a deep closed 
low over Quebec with a well-defined shortwave embedded over northern 
Ontario. This shortwave is going to pivot through the UP and Upper 
Great Lakes region over the next day, bringing a cold front and 
significant cold advection aloft for the region. With Lake Superior 
still at around 8 to 10 C and 850mb temperatures falling to -6 to -9 
C by midnight tonight, lake effect rain and eventually snow will 
form. A Winter Weather Advisory will go into effect overnight 
tonight as the high terrain of Baraga and Marquette Counties is 
still expected to see 4"-8" of snow throughout the next 2-3 days.

The greatest impact period starts overnight tonight as in addition 
to the aforementioned cooling temperatures aloft causing lake effect 
precip, surface temperatures will also fall sub-freezing. The main 
challenges with this forecast are temperatures, snow ratios, precip 
intensity (QPF) and the resulting accumulations when combining the 
QPF and snow ratios. While the current forecast of 4-8" above 1000' 
elevation (or about 400-600 ft above Lake Superior and higher) is 
still on the lower end of traditional criteria for a 48 hour span, 
the wet/slushy nature of the snow (at least initially) and expected 
occasional moderate-to-heavy rates (0.5-1.0+"/hr) support the first 
advisory of the 2026-27 winter season. Near the Lake Superior 
shoreline, warm flow onshore from an above-freezing Lake Superior 
will result in generally less than an inch of accumulation 
(including the city of Marquette). The best chance to see any 
accumulations there would be Thursday night when the 850mb temps 
fall to near -9C (REFS mean). Impacts to the area roads will be 
greatest during the overnight hours tonight and Thursday night, 
though periods of heavier snow during the daylight hours will still 
be impactful. 

For temperatures, the NBM continues to forecast much too cold for 
overnight temperatures as its bias-correction has been trained on 
recent stretches of cool, clear nights. This results in it having 
temperatures falling into the mid 20s over the interior and even 
below freezing at the immediate lakeshore tonight and Thursday 
night. This seems to be an unlikely scenario given the strong 
onshore flow from a warm lake, cloud cover, precipitation processes 
releasing latent heat, and only marginally cold 850mb temps of -6 to 
-10C. Overall thinking is that temperatures will remain above 
freezing overnight near the Lake Superior shoreline and much of the 
eastern U.P. tonight with slightly cooler temperatures Thursday 
night falling to right around freezing. 

SLRs also look quite a bit overdone in the NBM with 16:1 by Friday 
including over the Great Lakes. This again would be an unlikely 
scenario given the warmer low levels and warm ground temperatures 
(mid 40s) ongoing. Similar thermal profiles to last week's high 
terrain lake effect snowfall yielded between 5:1 and 7:1 SLR. These 
values seem reasonable for tonight into Thursday, then approaching 
10:1 Thursday night as cooling continues. A locally developed 
temperature-to-SLR curve matches up well with this for areas away 
from the lake with very low SLRs. Have bumped up SLRs some as REFS 
soundings interior from the Great Lakes do show inversion heights to 
around 8kft and saturation into the lower end of the DGZ, which 
would support periods of above 10:1 SLRs (without the above context 
of warmer temperatures, etc).

While confidence is high in achieving a low end advisory scenario, 
confidence is low with regards to higher end scenarios. While the 
coarse resolution models (LREF members) are producing a mean QPF of 
around one third to two thirds of an inch, the hi-res models such as 
the REFS members are much more aggressive with a mean QPF over the 
high terrain of Marquette and Baraga counties of over an inch. The 
75th percentile of the REFS (a "reasonable high-end solution") 
paints a bullseye of nearly 1.75" in the high terrain at the 
Baraga/Marquette County line. Even with lower end SLRs, this would 
yield warning criteria snowfall of 12-16" or more. REFS 
probabilities for 12"+ over the advisory period are in the 30-40% 
range for the highest terrain (well away from any US/MI highways in 
the McCormick Wilderness area). The area of strongest convergence 
will determine if these high-end scenarios are able to be realized. 
If convergent bands can reside over the same location for much of 
the next couple days, higher snow totals would be realized, but if 
those bands waver and wobble, the snow would be spread out over a 
wider area. As the global 500mb map still has notable spread in how
